items.summary: Diminution, foreshortening, convergence, and overlap are presented as general depth cues; overlap/foreshortening reinforce figure-specific canon but broaden its domain.
Perspective drawing is framed as representation of appearance from a viewpoint; lines of sight through a picture plane explain why the same object changes shape and size with viewpoint.
Cone of vision, central visual ray, and picture plane supply a causal model for the view and a boundary for later distortion discussion.
Each real parallel direction family not parallel to the picture plane converges toward its own vanishing point, located by a parallel sight direction from the observer.
All horizontal-world vanishing points lie on the observer's eye-level line; the line shifts within or beyond the frame as the observer looks straight out, down, or up.
One-, two-, and vertically convergent appearances follow object/view orientation; named perspective systems are consequences of direction families, not arbitrary styles.
Cubes/boxes are a general construction carrier for solving object orientation before complicated contour and detail.
Excessive convergence and edge deformation are controlled by a usable cone of vision, greater vanishing-point separation/viewing distance, or cropping; excessive separation can flatten the view.
Known heights can be carried through depth with vanishing guides; equal-height figures on the same level plane maintain a constant proportion to the observer's eye level.
Known widths can be transported through the same field, allowing consistent repeated object scale beyond figure-derived calibration.
Perspective-rectangle diagonals locate true centers and support equal subdivisions/repeated intervals even when visual midpoints and gaps are unequal on the page.
Measuring lines and a construction vanishing point can transfer arbitrary equal or unequal intervals into depth; this is a precision specialty rather than a compulsory first-line method.
A flat design can be transferred to a perspective plane by locating key points in a grid and reconstructing the grid in perspective.
Inclined plane directions use vanishing points directly above or below the corresponding horizontal-direction vanishing point, and equal slopes share an inclined vanishing line.
A circle turns into an ellipse in perspective, but the original circle's true projected center is found from the enclosing perspective square and need not match the ellipse's visual center.
Cylinder and cone axes must pass through the true projected center of their circular cross-sections; side edges meet the projected circle tangentially.
Shade and cast shadow are distinct; for sunlight, parallel rays and the receiving plane determine cast-shadow direction and intersections.
A local point source uses rays diverging from the source; the source's projection onto a plane helps determine shadow directions for upright forms.

items.summary: D'Amelio supplies the independent eye-level, vanishing-direction, measurement, and plane-construction foundation that the held figure-derived shared-scene Pattern explicitly says it does not replace.
The book's mathematics can be operationalized as visual construction checks—establish, project, intersect, subdivide—without requiring equations or formal geometry derivations at runtime.
